ego.name: Max Planck
ego.summary: Max Planck was a German theoretical physicist whose work on black-body radiation introduced energy quanta and laid the foundation for quantum physics. A professor at Kiel and Berlin, he received the 1918 Nobel Prize in Physics and became a leading figure in German scientific life.

connections.relationship_description: Planck's father was a law professor whose 1867 appointment in Munich moved the family from Kiel into a larger academic environment.
connections.notes: Wilhelm’s 1867 appointment to the Munich chair of civil procedure moved the family from Kiel into a larger academic environment.

connections.relationship_description: Planck’s mother, Emma Patzig, remained a close personal attachment throughout his life and continued to move in Munich’s academic circles after Wilhelm von Planck’s death.
shared_activities: Family life in Kiel and Munich
connections.notes: This record is for Planck’s mother, Emma Patzig, who died on 4 August 1914. It must remain distinct from his daughter Emma Planck, who died in childbirth in 1919.

connections.relationship_description: Planck's mathematics teacher at the Maximiliansgymnasium, who introduced him to astronomy, mechanics, and the conservation of energy as a fundamental law.
shared_activities: Early engagement with the conservation of energy
connections.notes: Planck later described Müller's presentation of energy conservation as deeply formative.

connections.relationship_description: Planck's principal physics professor in Munich, who trained him in experimental physics and advised him about the prospects of a career in physics.
shared_activities: Physics studies at the University of Munich
Experimental investigation of hydrogen diffusion through heated platinum
connections.notes: Jolly famously cautioned Planck that physics was nearly complete, but later examined his doctoral work.

connections.relationship_description: Although not Planck's formal instructor, Clausius's writings on thermodynamics and entropy became the decisive intellectual influence on Planck's early research program.
shared_activities: Research on entropy and the second law
connections.notes: Planck's sustained study of Clausius was more influential than his Berlin lectures.

connections.relationship_description: Planck attended Kirchhoff's Berlin lectures as a student and, in 1889, succeeded him in the Berlin chair associated with radiation research.
shared_activities: Lectures at the Friedrich Wilhelm University
Berlin theoretical-physics chair and radiation research tradition
connections.notes: Planck found Kirchhoff's lectures carefully prepared but dry; Kirchhoff died in 1887.

connections.relationship_description: Planck attended Helmholtz's lectures in Berlin and later sought his advice before declining a professorship at the Forestry Academy in Aschaffenburg.
shared_activities: Career consultation concerning the Aschaffenburg offer
connections.notes: Planck admired Helmholtz's stature but was disappointed by his lectures.

connections.relationship_description: Boltzmann was initially Planck's major intellectual opponent on the statistical interpretation of entropy, but his statistical relation between entropy and microscopic states became central to Planck's 1900 radiation derivation.
shared_activities: Debate over entropy and the second law of thermodynamics
Development of foundations for quantum theory
connections.notes: Planck initially resisted Boltzmann's probabilistic approach, then adopted its methods during the formulation of his radiation law.

connections.relationship_description: Planck's longtime friend, fiancée, and first wife; their marriage began as he established his independent professorial and domestic life in Kiel.
shared_activities: Marriage and household in Kiel and Berlin
Family life during Planck's Berlin professorship
connections.notes: They married on March 31, 1887; Marie died in 1909.

connections.relationship_description: Planck's eldest child with Marie Merck, whose death while serving in the German Army was one of the family's devastating wartime losses.
shared_activities: Family experiences during World War I
connections.notes: Karl was killed during World War I in 1916.

connections.relationship_description: One of Planck's twin daughters; her death in childbirth in 1917 was part of a sequence of severe family losses.
connections.notes: Grete's daughter was subsequently cared for within the extended family.

connections.relationship_description: Planck's younger son, who became a civil servant and a participant in the conservative resistance to Hitler; Planck unsuccessfully appealed directly to Adolf Hitler for his life after his arrest.
shared_activities: Family relationship during Erwin's political career
Efforts to save Erwin after the July 20 plot
connections.notes: Erwin was executed at Plötzensee Prison in January 1945.

connections.relationship_description: Rubens supplied the crucial long-wavelength black-body radiation measurements that Planck used to formulate and test his radiation law in 1900.
connections.notes: Rubens and his wife discussed new data with Planck over dinner on October 7, 1900; Rubens soon confirmed Planck's formula experimentally.

connections.relationship_description: Planck became an early supporter of Einstein's physics and, with Walther Nernst, helped recruit him from Zurich to Berlin in 1913; they later shared Berlin's scientific institutions and musical gatherings.
shared_activities: Recruitment of Einstein to Berlin and the Prussian Academy
connections.notes: Einstein's 1905 work extended the quantum concept introduced by Planck, while Planck helped provide Einstein an institutional base in Berlin.

connections.relationship_description: Nernst worked with Planck to persuade Einstein to move to Berlin and collaborated with him in building the institutional setting for twentieth-century German physics.
shared_activities: Planning the Kaiser Wilhelm Institute for Physics
connections.notes: Nernst and Planck jointly approached Einstein in Zurich in 1913 with the Berlin offer.

connections.relationship_description: Planck's second wife, whom he married after the death of Marie Merck; together they had a son, Hermann.
shared_activities: Family life through Planck's final decades
connections.notes: The available account identifies the marriage as beginning in 1911.

category_summaries.summary: Planck's family supplied both the academic culture and the private obligations that ran alongside his scientific career. His parents established the learned, Protestant middle-class environment that shaped his early confidence in scholarship, while his marriages and children anchored his years in Kiel and Berlin. The deaths of his first wife and three children, followed by Erwin's execution in 1945, made the contrast between Planck's public eminence and his private bereavements especially severe.

Planck's education was marked less by inspirational university lecturing than by formative ideas and independent study. At Munich, Hermann Müller made the conservation of energy a compelling intellectual principle, while Philipp von Jolly supplied rigorous experimental and institutional training. The decisive scholarly turn came through Planck's close reading of Clausius on entropy and the second law, a commitment he carried from his dissertation into the theoretical work that ultimately led toward quantum physics.

Planck's professional circle joined conceptual physics, exact experiment, and scientific institution-building. His early disagreement with Boltzmann gave way to a productive use of statistical reasoning, while Rubens's infrared measurements made the 1900 radiation law possible. In Berlin, Planck helped consolidate a new community of theoretical physics: he supported Einstein's work and, with Nernst, brought Einstein to the city in 1913, strengthening the network from which quantum theory and modern physics developed.
